cards.q: What are the four distinct problems that JavaScript's lack of types causes?
cards.a: Errors found late (only when that exact line runs with that exact value), editors that know nothing about your values, refactoring by text search rather than by meaning, and documentation in comments that silently rots.

cards.q: Why didn't teams just switch to Java or C# instead of inventing TypeScript?
cards.a: The JavaScript already existed, ran in browsers and Node, and depended on hundreds of thousands of untyped packages. Any solution had to run existing JavaScript, interoperate with untyped libraries, and be adoptable one file at a time.

cards.q: Who created TypeScript and when was it announced?
cards.a: Anders Hejlsberg at Microsoft, announced October 2012. He had previously designed Turbo Pascal, Delphi and C#.

cards.q: Why is 'the editor knows nothing' a serious problem rather than a comfort issue?
cards.a: Without type information the only way to learn what a value holds is to read the code that produced it, and then the code that produced that. It is the main reason developers cannot move quickly in unfamiliar codebases.

cards.q: Why does untyped code calcify over time?
cards.a: Renaming or reshaping something can only be done by text search, which cannot distinguish this email from an unrelated one. Refactoring becomes a gamble, so bad names and shapes survive for years.

cards.q: What is wrong with documenting a function's parameters in a comment?
cards.a: Nothing enforces it, so it is correct the day it is written and slowly becomes fiction. The only trustworthy documentation becomes the implementation, which defeats the purpose of an interface.

cards.q: What constraint most shaped TypeScript's design, and what did it rule out?
cards.a: That it had to describe JavaScript that already existed. This ruled out nominal typing, ruled out changing runtime semantics, and required gradual, file-by-file adoption.

cards.q: Give the canonical example of the class of bug TypeScript exists to prevent.
cards.a: A function reads user.email but a caller passes an object with emailAddress. Nothing complains, tests pass because they call it correctly, and it fails in production on a path nobody exercised.

cards.q: What is a type annotation?
cards.a: A claim about what a value is, written after a colon: let count: number = 0. The compiler checks every place the claim could be violated.

cards.q: Does tsc ever run your program?
cards.a: No. It reads the code, builds a model of what every expression's type must be, and compares that model against itself. Everything TypeScript knows, it knows from reading.

cards.q: What does TypeScript infer for let count = 0 versus const name = 'devansh'?
cards.a: count is inferred as number. name is inferred as the literal type 'devansh', because a const can never be reassigned so no other value is possible.

cards.q: Why does the let versus const inference difference matter later?
cards.a: Literal inference from const is what makes literal unions, discriminated unions and as const work. Without it every string would widen to string and narrowing would have nothing to distinguish.

cards.q: Where should you annotate, and where should you let inference work?
cards.a: Annotate where information enters the program — function parameters and the shapes of external data. Let inference carry it through everything in between.

cards.q: Why is over-annotating a real problem rather than harmless extra safety?
cards.a: It writes down things the compiler already knew, and those written-down facts then rot the way comments do. It also hides genuine inference errors behind your assertion of what you expected.

cards.q: By default, does tsc emit JavaScript when it finds type errors?
cards.a: Yes. Type errors are reported, not fatal, so that a codebase with thousands of errors can still ship during adoption. noEmitOnError changes this.

cards.q: Why does 'it ran' prove nothing about whether code type-checked?
cards.a: Because emit is independent of checking by default, and because most real projects use a transpile-only tool that never checks at all, with tsc --noEmit as a separate gate.

cards.q: How does inference flow through an expression like 'a,b'.split(',')?
cards.a: TypeScript ships type declarations for every built-in JavaScript function, so it knows String.prototype.split returns string[] and infers that for the result.

cards.q: What does a well-typed TypeScript file usually look like in terms of annotation density?
cards.a: Annotations at the edges only — parameters and external data shapes — with everything internal inferred. A file dense with annotations is usually a smell.

cards.q: You annotate const ids: string[] = [] and later push numbers by mistake — caught or not?
cards.a: Caught. The annotation fixes the element type, so the push is an error. Without the annotation an empty array literal infers as never[] or widens under evolving-array inference, which behaves differently.

cards.q: Why does an empty array sometimes accept anything and sometimes accept nothing?
cards.a: With an annotation it is fixed. Without one, in a let or var with no annotation, TypeScript uses evolving array inference and learns the element type from what you push; in other positions it becomes never[].

cards.q: What is type widening?
cards.a: When a literal type is generalised to its base type — 'a' becomes string on assignment to a mutable binding. as const and satisfies are the tools for preventing it.

cards.q: What does it mean that TypeScript is structurally typed?
cards.a: A value is compatible with a type if it has the right shape — the right properties with the right types — regardless of what it was declared as or what class it came from. No declared intention to be compatible is needed.

cards.q: What is nominal typing and which languages use it?
cards.a: Compatibility requires a declared relationship by name — this class implements that interface. Java and C# work this way.

cards.q: Why did TypeScript choose structural over nominal typing?
cards.a: JavaScript code is written with object literals and duck typing everywhere. A nominal system would have rejected virtually all existing JavaScript as untyped, defeating the adoption goal.

cards.q: What practical problem does structural typing create with IDs?
cards.a: If UserId and PostId are both string, nothing prevents passing one where the other belongs, because they are structurally identical. Branded types are the workaround.

cards.q: What is excess property checking, and why does it seem to contradict structural typing?
cards.a: Passing an object literal directly with unknown extra properties is an error, even though structurally extra properties are fine. It is a deliberate special case because a fresh literal with an extra property is nearly always a typo.

cards.q: Why does assigning a literal to a variable first make an excess property error disappear?
cards.a: The check only applies to fresh object literals at the assignment or call site. Once stored in a variable the value is no longer fresh, and ordinary structural rules apply.

cards.q: What does erasure mean in TypeScript?
cards.a: Every annotation, interface and generic parameter is deleted at compile time. The output is JavaScript with types stripped and nothing added — no runtime library, no runtime type information.

cards.q: Why was erasure a deliberate design constraint?
cards.a: The emitted code had to be clean, readable JavaScript with no runtime cost, so adopting TypeScript could never be blamed for slowing anything down.

cards.q: Name the two biggest consequences of erasure.
cards.a: You cannot check a type at runtime — there is no if (x is User) — and types cannot influence what the program does, so generics never generate specialized code.

cards.q: Why can't typeof or instanceof tell you whether an object matches an interface?
cards.a: They are JavaScript operators that predate TypeScript. typeof only distinguishes primitives plus function and object; instanceof checks the prototype chain, so it only works for class or constructor-built values.

cards.q: Do generics generate specialized code the way C++ templates do?
cards.a: No. There is exactly one function at runtime; the type parameter is gone. You cannot write new T() or ask what T was.

cards.q: A function expects { name: string } and you pass an object with name and age stored in a variable. Error or not?
cards.a: Not an error. Structural typing accepts extra properties; only fresh object literals trigger excess property checking.

cards.q: How would you make two string-based ID types incompatible?
cards.a: Brand them: type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }, constructed only through a function that asserts the brand.

cards.q: Why is 'can I check at runtime whether this object is a User?' always answered no?
cards.a: Because interfaces are erased. Nothing about a plain object at runtime records which interface it satisfied at compile time.

cards.q: What is the practical difference between an interface and a type alias for describing an object?
cards.a: Almost none — both are structural, erased, and checked identically. The real differences are that interfaces merge and type aliases can express unions, tuples, primitives and computed types.

cards.q: What does it mean that interfaces merge?
cards.a: Declaring the same interface twice in a scope produces one interface with the union of the members. Type aliases collide and error instead.

cards.q: Why does interface merging matter beyond being a quirk?
cards.a: It is the mechanism behind module augmentation — how you add a property to a type inside someone else's package, which is how Fastify plugins and Express middleware type their additions.

cards.q: What is the usual working rule for choosing between interface and type alias?
cards.a: Interfaces for object shapes others may extend, type aliases for everything else. Consistency within a codebase matters more than the choice.

cards.q: What does an optional property with ? actually do to the type?
cards.a: It makes the property possibly absent and gives it the type T | undefined, which is why you must narrow before using it under strictNullChecks.

cards.q: Is readonly enforced at runtime?
cards.a: No. The compiler rejects assignment but the property is fully writable at runtime. Object.freeze is the unrelated runtime equivalent.

cards.q: What does an index signature buy you and what does it cost?
cards.a: { [key: string]: number } describes a dictionary with arbitrary keys. The cost is that you lose all knowledge of which keys exist, so every lookup is a maybe.

cards.q: What is an intersection type?
cards.a: A & B means a value has all the members of both. It is the type-alias equivalent of interface B extends A for most practical purposes.

cards.q: What happens when an intersection has conflicting members, like {a: string} & {a: number}?
cards.a: The property becomes never rather than producing an error at the declaration. That silent never often surfaces as a confusing error several files away.

cards.q: Why does one entity often need several object types rather than one?
cards.a: Because the shape differs by direction across a boundary — a row you read has an id and timestamps, a row you write does not, and an API response may hide fields the database holds.

cards.q: When would you deliberately choose a type alias over an interface for an object?
cards.a: When the type is a union member, when it is computed with mapped or conditional types, or when you specifically want to prevent third-party augmentation.

cards.q: How do you express 'an object with these known keys plus arbitrary extras'?
cards.a: Combine known properties with an index signature, or use an intersection. Note that the index signature's value type must be compatible with every declared property's type.

cards.q: Why does adding an index signature often break existing property types?
cards.a: Because every declared property must be assignable to the index signature's value type, so a mixed-type object needs the index value type widened to a union.

cards.q: What is a union type and why is it the feature that lets TypeScript describe JavaScript at all?
cards.a: A | B means the value is one of several types. JavaScript code constantly returns a value or null, accepts a string or a number, and branches on what it got; without unions none of that is expressible.

cards.q: Why can't you call x.toUpperCase() when x: string | number?
cards.a: A union only permits operations valid for every member. Until you prove which member you hold, only the common surface is available.

cards.q: What is narrowing?
cards.a: TypeScript's control flow analysis: it reads your branches and, inside a branch, knows more about a value than it did outside. It is what makes unions usable.

cards.q: List the main narrowing devices.
cards.a: typeof for primitives, instanceof for class instances, the in operator for property presence, truthiness checks, equality against literals, Array.isArray, and user-defined type predicates.

cards.q: How does an early return narrow the rest of a function?
cards.a: Narrowing survives return, throw and else, so once the null case has returned, the remainder of the function sees the narrowed type without further checks.

cards.q: What is a literal type?
cards.a: A type inhabited by exactly one value, such as 'pending' or 42. On its own it is a curiosity; unioned it becomes a checked set of allowed values.

cards.q: Why do experienced TypeScript teams use string literal unions where a Java developer reaches for an enum?
cards.a: They give the same closed set of values with autocomplete and compile-time checking, at zero runtime cost, and they narrow naturally. Enums emit runtime code and numeric ones are unsound.

cards.q: What is a discriminated union?
cards.a: A union of object types where every member has a common property whose type is a distinct literal, so checking that one property narrows the whole object.

cards.q: Give three real things best modelled as a discriminated union.
cards.a: A fetch result (success with data, failure with error), a job state (queued, running, succeeded, failed), and a message protocol where each message kind carries different fields.

cards.q: How does exhaustiveness checking work?
cards.a: Switch on the discriminant, handle every case, and in the default branch assign the value to a variable of type never. If a new member is added and not handled, that assignment fails to compile.

cards.q: Why is exhaustiveness checking the payoff of the whole type system?
cards.a: It turns adding a case into a compiler-generated list of every place that must change — the change-one-thing-and-be-told-what-else-breaks experience that makes static typing worth the cost.

cards.q: Why does narrowing get forgotten after you call a function?
cards.a: TypeScript is conservative: the call might have reassigned a mutable property, so it can no longer prove the narrowing holds. Copying the narrowed value into a const first is the usual fix.

cards.q: How do you model an operation that can fail without exceptions?
cards.a: A Result discriminated union — { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: E } — so the caller cannot read the data without first checking, and the compiler enforces it.

cards.q: What is the difference between a union and an intersection in one line?
cards.a: A union is 'one of these', an intersection is 'all of these at once'. Unions restrict what you can do until narrowed; intersections combine members.

cards.q: Why does discriminating on a boolean property work as well as on a string?
cards.a: Because true and false are themselves literal types, so { ok: true } and { ok: false } are distinguishable members.

cards.q: When does in narrowing fail to do what you want?
cards.a: When both union members could have the property, or when the property is optional on one — presence then does not uniquely identify the member. An explicit discriminant is more reliable than structural sniffing.

cards.q: You narrow obj.value with a typeof check, call a helper, then use it — and the narrowing is gone. Why, and what is the fix?
cards.a: The helper could have reassigned the property, so the compiler cannot prove the narrowing still holds. Copy the narrowed value into a const before the call.

cards.q: Your never exhaustiveness check stopped erroring after you added a union member. What likely happened?
cards.a: Something upstream widened the type — often an any, an assertion, or a member typed string instead of a literal — so the default branch no longer receives never.

cards.q: Why does discriminating on an optional property behave badly?
cards.a: Because absence and a member that happens to lack the property are not distinguishable enough to narrow reliably. A required discriminant with distinct literals is the robust design.

cards.q: How do you narrow a union of objects with no common discriminant?
cards.a: With the in operator on a property unique to one member, or by adding a discriminant. Adding the discriminant is almost always better than sniffing structure.

cards.q: What did TypeScript do with null and undefined before strictNullChecks?
cards.a: They were assignable to every type, so a string could be null. This existed so that mountains of existing JavaScript would not be flagged as broken.

cards.q: What does strictNullChecks change, and when did it arrive?
cards.a: TypeScript 2.0, in 2016. Null and undefined get their own types and are only allowed where you declared them, so a possibly-missing value becomes a union you must narrow.

cards.q: Why is strictNullChecks the highest-value single flag?
cards.a: It points at exactly the places a null-reference crash can occur, eliminating the largest class of production runtime errors at compile time.

cards.q: Why is turning it on so disruptive for an existing codebase?
cards.a: Every place that implicitly relied on null flowing anywhere becomes an error at once, which is often thousands of errors — which is why teams postpone it and why it lives behind a flag.

cards.q: What does optional chaining a?.b?.c return when something in the chain is nullish?
cards.a: undefined, instead of throwing — and the resulting type includes undefined, so the compiler still makes you handle it.

cards.q: Why does ?? exist alongside ||?
cards.a: ?? supplies a default only for null and undefined, while || also fires on 0 and the empty string. Using || for defaults silently discards legitimate falsy values.

cards.q: What is strict and what does it turn on?
cards.a: A single flag enabling the whole strict family: noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, useUnknownInCatchVariables and alwaysStrict.

cards.q: What does noImplicitAny do and why is it second in value only to null checks?
cards.a: It errors when a parameter's type cannot be inferred rather than silently making it any. Without it the compiler quietly inserts the one thing that disables checking.

cards.q: What does strictPropertyInitialization require?
cards.a: That every class field is actually assigned — in the declaration, in the constructor, or explicitly marked as possibly undefined or definitely assigned.

cards.q: Why is a caught error unknown under useUnknownInCatchVariables?
cards.a: Because JavaScript can throw any value, including a string or a number. Assuming err.message exists is how error handlers throw their own errors.

cards.q: What does noUncheckedIndexedAccess do and why is it outside strict?
cards.a: It makes arr[0] typed T | undefined, which is technically correct because indices can be out of range. It is excluded because it produces a great deal of friction for a comparatively narrow class of bugs.

cards.q: Why is 'is this valid TypeScript?' not a well-formed question?
cards.a: Because behaviour is configuration-dependent. The same file can compile cleanly in one repo and produce forty errors in another, depending on which strict flags are set.

cards.q: What is the historical story you can tell about null in an interview?
cards.a: Tony Hoare called the null reference his billion-dollar mistake. strictNullChecks is the correction: it makes absence a distinct type you must handle rather than a value hiding inside every type.

cards.q: What does exactOptionalPropertyTypes distinguish?
cards.a: Between a property that is absent and one explicitly set to undefined. Without it both are the same to the checker, which matters when code branches on in or spreads objects.

cards.q: You enable strict on an existing project and get 900 errors. What is the sane order of attack?
cards.a: Fix implicit any parameters first, since they unblock inference everywhere else, then possibly-undefined accesses by module, and treat each ! you add as debt to revisit rather than a fix.

cards.q: Why is x?.y! a contradiction worth flagging in review?
cards.a: Optional chaining says this may be missing, the non-null assertion says it definitely is not. One of the two is wrong, and the assertion silences the check the chain just performed.

cards.q: What is the difference between foo?.() and foo() when foo may be undefined?
cards.a: The optional call invokes only if foo is not nullish, returning undefined otherwise, which keeps the type honest instead of requiring a guard or an assertion.

cards.q: Should you annotate a function's return type?
cards.a: Usually let it be inferred so it stays honest as the body changes — except for exported public API functions, where an explicit return type protects the published contract, improves error messages and speeds up compilation.

cards.q: What is contextual typing?
cards.a: When a function is written where its type is already known — a callback to .map, a handler assigned to a typed field — its parameters take their types from that context and need no annotation.

cards.q: Why does extracting an inline arrow function to a standalone const suddenly produce an implicit any error?
cards.a: Because it loses its context. Inline, the parameter type came from the surrounding expression; standalone there is nothing to infer from.

cards.q: What is the difference between b?: number and b = 0 in a parameter list?
cards.a: The optional parameter has type number | undefined inside the body. The defaulted parameter is optional at the call site but remains number inside.

cards.q: Are function return types covariant or contravariant, and what does that mean?
cards.a: Covariant: a function returning Dog is usable where one returning Animal is expected, because every caller expecting an animal still gets one.

cards.q: Are function parameters covariant or contravariant, and why?
cards.a: Contravariant: a function accepting Animal is usable where one accepting Dog is expected, because it can handle everything the specific one could and more. The reverse is unsafe.

cards.q: What is the bivariance hole in method parameters?
cards.a: Method-syntax parameters are checked in both directions, which is unsound. It was kept deliberately because array and DOM types in the real world depend on it.

cards.q: What exactly does strictFunctionTypes fix and what does it leave alone?
cards.a: It restores correct contravariance for function-property syntax such as handler: (e: Event) => void, but leaves method syntax handler(e: Event): void bivariant.

cards.q: Why is the bivariance hole a good interview answer rather than an embarrassment?
cards.a: Because the honest answer includes why: TypeScript accepted some unsoundness to remain usable on real JavaScript, and being able to name a deliberate trade shows you understand the system's goals.

cards.q: What are function overloads and what is the rule about the implementation signature?
cards.a: Several call signatures declared before one implementation. The implementation signature must be compatible with all of them and is not itself callable from outside.

cards.q: When should you prefer a union or a generic over overloads?
cards.a: Almost always in modern TypeScript. Overloads do not narrow well, are easy to get subtly wrong, and a well-typed generic or a union usually expresses the same relationship more clearly.

cards.q: How do you type this in a standalone function?
cards.a: With a fake first parameter — function f(this: HTMLElement, e: Event) — which is erased at compile time and exists to state what the call site must be.

cards.q: Why do function types need rules at all, rather than just matching by shape?
cards.a: Because substituting one function for another is safe only in specific directions; getting it wrong is how code that compiles cleanly still crashes when a handler is called with an input it cannot handle.

cards.q: What does a rest parameter's type look like and where can it appear?
cards.a: ...args: number[], and only in the final position. With tuple types it can express a fixed head and a variadic tail.

cards.q: You pass a handler typed (e: MouseEvent) => void where (e: Event) => void is expected. Sound or unsound?
cards.a: Unsound — the handler will receive events that are not mouse events. TypeScript allows it for method-syntax positions because of bivariance, which is exactly the hole to be able to name.

cards.q: Why do callbacks that ignore extra arguments type-check fine?
cards.a: Because a function with fewer parameters is assignable where one with more is expected — extra arguments are simply unused, which is safe and matches how JavaScript callbacks are written.

cards.q: When does an inferred return type surprise you?
cards.a: When a function returns different types on different branches and inference produces a wide union, or when it returns an object literal whose properties widen. An explicit return type both documents and constrains.

cards.q: Is there any difference between T[] and Array<T>?
cards.a: No — they are identical. Pick one and be consistent across the codebase.

cards.q: Why does .filter(Boolean) not remove null from the element type?
cards.a: Because TypeScript cannot see that Boolean narrows. You need a type predicate such as (x): x is T => x != null for the type to follow the runtime behaviour.

cards.q: Why does .reduce so often need an explicit type?
cards.a: Inference takes the accumulator type from the initial value, which is frequently too narrow — an empty array or object infers as never[] or {}.

cards.q: What is a tuple type?
cards.a: A fixed-length array where each position has its own type, such as [string, number]. It types things like useState returns and coordinate pairs.

cards.q: What can tuples do beyond fixed positions?
cards.a: Optional elements, rest elements such as [string, ...number[]], and labels such as [x: number, y: number] which exist purely to improve editor hints.

cards.q: Is tuple-ness enforced at runtime?
cards.a: No. At runtime it is an ordinary array and nothing stops .push from lengthening it. Declaring it readonly makes the compiler prevent that.

cards.q: What does as const do to a literal?
cards.a: Makes it maximally narrow and deeply readonly — ['a','b'] as const becomes readonly ['a','b'], and object properties get literal types instead of widened ones.

cards.q: How do you derive a union type from an as const array?
cards.a: typeof arr[number] — indexed access with number gives the union of element types, which for an as const array is the union of its literals.

cards.q: What duplication does as const eliminate?
cards.a: Maintaining a runtime list of allowed values and a matching union type by hand. With as const the array is the source and the type is computed from it, so they cannot drift.

cards.q: Why is array covariance a soundness hole?
cards.a: TypeScript lets you treat Dog[] as Animal[], and then pushing a Cat into it type-checks while corrupting the original array. It was accepted because forbidding it breaks too much real code.

cards.q: What does readonly T[] actually prevent?
cards.a: Calls to mutating methods and index assignment at compile time. It does not freeze anything at runtime, and a readonly array is not assignable to a mutable one.

cards.q: How do you get the element type out of an array type?
cards.a: Indexed access with number: T[number]. The same idiom works on tuples to get the union of their element types.

cards.q: Why is [1, 2] as const useful when passing to a function expecting a tuple?
cards.a: Without it the argument infers as number[], which is not assignable to [number, number] because length is not guaranteed.

cards.q: How do you type a function that returns a tuple so destructuring works well?
cards.a: Annotate the return as a tuple type or use as const on the returned literal; otherwise it infers as an array union and destructured names all get the union type.

cards.q: What does satisfies do for an as const registry object?
cards.a: Checks each entry against a shape while preserving the literal keys and values, so you get validation and still derive precise unions from the object.

cards.q: What problem do generics solve that any cannot?
cards.a: They preserve the relationship between input and output. (arr: any[]) => any throws the answer away; <T>(arr: T[]) => T | undefined gives the caller back their own type.

cards.q: What is the simplest correct mental model for a generic?
cards.a: A function that takes types as arguments and returns a type. Same idea as an ordinary function, one level up.

cards.q: Do you usually pass type arguments explicitly?
cards.a: No. TypeScript infers them from the values at the call site. You write them explicitly only when inference cannot get there or gets it wrong.

cards.q: Why is an unconstrained T nearly useless inside a function body?
cards.a: Because T could be anything, so no property access or operation is safe — you cannot even read .length.

cards.q: What does extends mean in <T extends { length: number }>?
cards.a: Is assignable to — the structural relation, not class inheritance. It restricts T to types that at least have that shape, while still returning the caller's precise type.

cards.q: Write from memory the signature of a fully type-safe property getter.
cards.a: function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] — the key must be a real key of the object and the return type is that key's value type.

cards.q: What is a default type parameter and when is it useful?
cards.a: <T = string> supplies a type when the caller does not. Useful for library APIs where a common case should not require an explicit argument.

cards.q: Where can generics appear besides functions?
cards.a: On interfaces, type aliases and classes — interface Box<T>, Map<string, User>, Promise<Response>. You have been using generic types long before writing one.

cards.q: What is the rule of thumb about a type parameter used in only one place?
cards.a: It is probably doing nothing. The value of a generic is in linking two positions; a T that appears once could usually be unknown or a union.

cards.q: Can you construct a value of type T inside a generic function?
cards.a: No. T is erased, so new T() is impossible. If you need construction, take a factory or a constructor type as a parameter instead.

cards.q: What happens to a generic when you pass it an any?
cards.a: The type parameter becomes any, and checking is disabled downstream for everything derived from it. This is one of the main ways any spreads.

cards.q: How do generic constraints interact with narrowing?
cards.a: A constrained T is treated as its constraint for member access, but the value's actual type stays T, which is why returning a modified object often needs care rather than just returning the constraint's shape.

cards.q: What is a common sign a generic is over-engineered?
cards.a: Three or more type parameters where one is always inferred to the same thing, or a signature you cannot read aloud. Simplify by making a parameter concrete or replacing it with a union.

cards.q: What does it mean that generic type arguments are inferred 'at the call site'?
cards.a: Each call independently determines the type arguments from the values passed. There is no single instantiation shared across calls, because at runtime there is only one function anyway.

cards.q: Inference picked a wider type than you wanted for T. What are your options?
cards.a: Pass the type argument explicitly, add as const at the call site, use a const type parameter, or constrain T so the inference site is narrower.

cards.q: What does a const type parameter do?
cards.a: <const T>, added in TypeScript 5.0, makes inference behave as though the argument had as const, preserving literal types without the caller writing it.

cards.q: What is NoInfer<T> for?
cards.a: Excluding a position from inference so that a type parameter is decided by the argument you intended, typically when a default value should not widen the parameter it belongs to.

cards.q: How do you type a function generic over an object and one of its keys, returning the value?
cards.a: <T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]. Both parameters link, which is what makes the generic worth having.

cards.q: What does any actually do?
cards.a: Turns checking off for that value. Anything is assignable to it, it is assignable to anything, and every property access on it succeeds and yields any.

cards.q: Why is any described as contagious?
cards.a: It propagates through every expression it touches — into generics, into spread objects, into derived values — so a single any can silently disable checking across a whole module.

cards.q: What is unknown and how does it differ from any?
cards.a: It also accepts any value, but you can do nothing with it until you narrow. It is the type-safe top type: I do not know what this is, and the compiler will force me to find out.

cards.q: Where should unknown be your default?
cards.a: Anywhere external data enters — parsed JSON, worker messages, caught errors, LLM output. Every place you are tempted to write any for incoming data.

cards.q: Name the four places never shows up.
cards.a: The return type of a function that never returns normally; a branch the compiler has proven unreachable; the result of an impossible intersection; and as the identity element of unions, where string | never is just string.

cards.q: What is the assignability relationship for never?
cards.a: never is assignable to everything, and nothing is assignable to never — exactly the reverse of any and unknown.

cards.q: What is a type assertion and what does it check?
cards.a: value as User tells the compiler to trust you. Nothing is checked at compile time or runtime, and no conversion happens — it is a claim, not a cast.

cards.q: What does as unknown as X signal?
cards.a: That the two types are unrelated enough for TypeScript to refuse a direct assertion. It is a loud sign that something upstream is wrong, not a technique to reach for.

cards.q: Why is the angle-bracket assertion syntax unusable in .tsx files?
cards.a: Because <User>value collides with JSX syntax. Use as everywhere for consistency.

cards.q: What is the non-null assertion and why is it dangerous?
cards.a: x! claims a value is not null or undefined without any check. It is the most common source of runtime null errors in strict codebases, because each one overrides the exact protection you enabled.

cards.q: What is a type predicate?
cards.a: A function returning x is User, which the compiler trusts for narrowing. It concentrates the unsafe claim in one auditable place instead of scattering assertions at every use.

cards.q: What is an assertion function?
cards.a: function assertIsUser(x: unknown): asserts x is User — it narrows for the rest of the enclosing scope by throwing rather than returning a boolean.

cards.q: What does satisfies do that an annotation does not?
cards.a: It checks a value against a type without widening it, so the precise inferred type is preserved. An annotation validates and then replaces the inferred type with the declared one.

cards.q: When was satisfies added and what pattern does it replace?
cards.a: TypeScript 4.9, in 2022. It replaces a large amount of code that used as purely to keep literal precision while still getting some checking.

cards.q: Give a concrete case where satisfies is clearly right.
cards.a: A config object that must conform to a Config type but whose exact keys you want to keep for deriving a union later — annotate and you lose the keys, assert and you lose the checking, satisfies keeps both.

cards.q: How should you handle a caught error properly?
cards.a: Treat it as unknown, narrow with instanceof Error or a type predicate for your own error classes, and have a fallback path for values that are neither.

cards.q: You are given data: any from a legacy helper. What is the minimal responsible change?
cards.a: Change the helper's return to unknown and validate at the one call site, rather than leaving any to spread through everything downstream.

cards.q: Why is a type predicate safer than an assertion even though both are unchecked claims?
cards.a: The predicate is one function you can test and audit; assertions are scattered claims at every use site with no shared implementation to review.

cards.q: How do you write a type predicate that actually checks?
cards.a: Inspect the value at runtime and return a boolean: check it is an object, not null, and that each required property exists with the right typeof. The signature only tells the compiler what your check proves.

cards.q: What does never in an error message usually mean in practice?
cards.a: That the compiler proved a case impossible — often because a union member was excluded by narrowing, or because an intersection conflicted. Read it as 'nothing can be here'.

cards.q: What kind of language is TypeScript's type system?
cards.a: A pure, functional, lazily-evaluated programming language in which you compute new types from existing types. It is Turing-complete in practice, which is both its power and its danger.

cards.q: What does keyof produce?
cards.a: The union of a type's keys — keyof User is 'name' | 'email'.

cards.q: How does typeof in type position differ from the JavaScript operator?
cards.a: They share a spelling and nothing else. In type position it lifts a value's inferred type into type space, so typeof config is the type of that value.

cards.q: What does indexed access do?
cards.a: Reads a property's type: User['email'] is string. With number on an array it gives the element type.

cards.q: How do you derive a union of an object's values?
cards.a: typeof obj[keyof typeof obj] — take the value's type, take its keys, index into it with all of them.

cards.q: What is a mapped type?
cards.a: { [K in keyof T]: ... } — a transformation applied to every member of a shape, optionally changing the value type, the optionality or the readonly-ness.

cards.q: What do the -? and -readonly modifiers do in a mapped type?
cards.a: They remove optionality and remove readonly respectively, which is how Required<T> and a mutable-ising utility are written.

cards.q: Name the utility types you should know cold and what each does.
cards.a: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited, NonNullable, Exclude and Extract.

cards.q: How would you write Pick from scratch?
cards.a: type Pick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] } — a mapped type over a constrained subset of keys.

cards.q: How would you write Omit from scratch?
cards.a: type Omit<T, K> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>> — everything except the named keys, which is why it composes Exclude.

cards.q: What is a conditional type?
cards.a: T extends U ? X : Y — the if of type space, where extends again means assignable to.

cards.q: What is distribution in a conditional type?
cards.a: A conditional over a naked type parameter applies to each union member separately and re-unions the results. That is how Exclude filters a union — non-matching members become never and vanish.

cards.q: How do you stop a conditional type from distributing?
cards.a: Wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y. You will need this the first time distribution surprises you.

cards.q: What does infer do?
cards.a: Declares a type variable captured by pattern matching inside a conditional type — T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T extracts what a promise resolves to.

cards.q: Which built-in utilities are written with infer?
cards.a: ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited, InstanceType and ConstructorParameters.

cards.q: What are template literal types good for?
cards.a: String manipulation in type space — building 'onClick' from 'click', typing route parameter objects from a path string, or constraining a string to a pattern.

cards.q: What is key remapping in a mapped type?
cards.a: Using as inside the mapping to rename keys — { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K & string>}`]: () => T[K] }. Mapping a key to never removes it.

cards.q: What are branded types and why do they need type-level tricks?
cards.a: A way to fake nominal typing by intersecting a primitive with an impossible marker property, so UserId and PostId stop being interchangeable despite both being strings.

cards.q: What is the danger of type-level programming, stated as a rule?
cards.a: A clever type nobody on the team can modify is a liability. Use the built-in utilities freely, write a simple mapped or conditional type to remove real duplication, and treat anything needing a comment to explain as a design smell.

cards.q: Does any of this produce runtime code?
cards.a: No. It is all erased. Type-level programming is an elaborate way of arranging compile-time checks and nothing else.

cards.q: Your conditional type behaves oddly on a union argument. What is the first thing to check?
cards.a: Whether distribution is happening. A naked type parameter distributes over unions; wrap in a tuple to stop it if you want the union treated as a whole.

cards.q: How do you make a mapped type that drops keys rather than transforming them?
cards.a: Use key remapping with as and map unwanted keys to never, which removes them from the resulting type.

cards.q: How would you type a path string so /users/:id produces { id: string }?
cards.a: A recursive template literal type that infers the segment after a colon and intersects it with the result of recursing on the rest of the string.

cards.q: Why prefer built-in utility types over hand-rolled equivalents?
cards.a: They are correct, familiar to every reader, and maintained. A hand-rolled Omit is another thing to debug for no benefit.

cards.q: What is the practical limit you should impose on recursive types?
cards.a: A hard depth cap, so a mistake produces a clear failure rather than a compiler error about excessive instantiation depth or a hung editor.

cards.q: Are private and protected enforced at runtime?
cards.a: No. They are compile-time only, and a private field is fully readable at runtime and appears in JSON.stringify.

cards.q: How does JavaScript's #private differ from TypeScript's private?
cards.a: #private is a runtime language feature genuinely inaccessible from outside the class. TypeScript's private is an erased compile-time annotation. They coexist and mean different things.

cards.q: What does implements actually do?
cards.a: Checks that the class structurally satisfies the interface. It does not create a nominal relationship — a different class with the same shape is still assignable.

cards.q: What is a parameter property?
cards.a: constructor(private name: string) — declares and assigns a field in one stroke. It is TypeScript-only syntax that emits an assignment, which is why it is not erasable.

cards.q: Why are enums the odd feature out in TypeScript?
cards.a: They emit a runtime object. Every other type-level construct disappears at compile time; an enum exists in the output JavaScript.

cards.q: What is unsound about numeric enums?
cards.a: For historical reasons any number is assignable to a numeric enum type in many positions, so a value that is not a member of the enum passes the check.

cards.q: What is a reverse mapping in a numeric enum?
cards.a: The emitted object maps both name to value and value back to name, so Status[0] yields 'Active'. String enums do not get this.

cards.q: What should you use instead of an enum, and why?
cards.a: A union of string literals, usually derived from an as const object. Same closed set with narrowing and autocomplete, no runtime emit, and compatible with type-stripping runtimes.

cards.q: What are namespaces and should you write new ones?
cards.a: TypeScript's pre-ES-modules module system. Legacy — you will meet them in old code and in declaration files, but should not write new ones.

cards.q: What is the state of decorators in TypeScript?
cards.a: There was a decade-old experimental version behind experimentalDecorators, and TypeScript 5.0 shipped the standardized ECMAScript version. They are not fully compatible, so you must know which flavour a codebase uses.

cards.q: Which frameworks depend heavily on decorators?
cards.a: Angular, NestJS and TypeORM. If you work on any of those, decorator flavour and metadata emission become practical concerns.

cards.q: Which TypeScript constructs are not erasable, and why does that matter now?
cards.a: Enums, parameter properties and namespaces. They emit runtime code, so they are incompatible with runtimes that strip types, which is why erasableSyntaxOnly exists.

cards.q: What does abstract give you?
cards.a: A class that cannot be instantiated and may declare members without implementations that subclasses must provide. Purely a compile-time constraint.

cards.q: When are classes genuinely the right tool in a TypeScript backend?
cards.a: Error hierarchies where instanceof narrowing is useful, and framework-mandated structures such as NestJS providers. Most data modelling is better served by plain object types and unions.

cards.q: How do you get exhaustive narrowing over a set of error classes?
cards.a: Give each a literal discriminant property, or use instanceof checks with a final never assignment. A discriminant survives across process boundaries; instanceof does not.

cards.q: Why does instanceof fail on errors that crossed a boundary?
cards.a: Serialisation loses the prototype — a thrown error sent through a worker, a queue or an HTTP response arrives as a plain object, so class identity is gone and only data-based discriminants survive.

cards.q: What replaces an enum in an erasable codebase?
cards.a: An as const object plus a union derived from its values, giving named constants at runtime and a closed literal union at compile time.

cards.q: What does import type do?
cards.a: States that an import is types only, so the emitted JavaScript drops it entirely rather than leaving a runtime import for something that does not exist at runtime.

cards.q: What problem does verbatimModuleSyntax solve?
cards.a: Ambiguity about which imports get elided. It keeps exactly what you wrote and requires import type where you mean types, which also makes single-file transpilers correct.

cards.q: What is a declaration file?
cards.a: A .d.ts file containing types with no implementations — a description of what some JavaScript elsewhere provides.

cards.q: How do you produce declaration files from your own source?
cards.a: tsc with declaration: true. Only tsc can emit them; esbuild, swc and other transpilers cannot.

cards.q: What are the three ways an npm package can have types?
cards.a: Bundled with the package and pointed at by types or the exports map; published separately on DefinitelyTyped as @types/name; or absent, in which case you write your own or declare it as any.

cards.q: What is DefinitelyTyped and what is the catch?
cards.a: A community repository of type declarations for JavaScript-only packages, published as @types/*. They are volunteer-written, versioned separately from the library, and can be wrong or stale.

cards.q: How do you debug 'my editor does not know about this library'?
cards.a: Check in order: does the package ship its own types, is there an @types package, and does your moduleResolution match how the package declares its entry points.

cards.q: What does the declare keyword mean?
cards.a: This exists, I am not defining it. It is how you describe ambient globals, modules you do not control, or non-JavaScript imports such as CSS files.

cards.q: Why has module resolution been through several incompatible eras?
cards.a: Because CommonJS and ES modules have genuinely different semantics, and TypeScript must describe both plus the interop layer. node, node16/nodenext and bundler each model a different reality.

cards.q: When should you use moduleResolution: bundler?
cards.a: When a bundler resolves your imports rather than Node — which is most frontend projects. It permits extensionless relative imports that nodenext would reject.

cards.q: What does esModuleInterop do?
cards.a: Makes CommonJS modules without a real default export importable with default-import syntax, by emitting interop helpers. It is on in most modern configs and changes what a default import means.

cards.q: Why do relative imports need file extensions under nodenext?
cards.a: Because that is what Node's ESM resolver requires at runtime, and TypeScript refuses to let you write an import that would fail when executed.

cards.q: What is the difference between augmenting a module and declaring one?
cards.a: declare module 'x' inside a file with imports or exports augments the existing module; in a file with none, it declares a whole new ambient module, which silently shadows rather than extends.

cards.q: Can a package ship working JavaScript and broken types?
cards.a: Yes, and it is common — a mismatched exports map or a missing types condition means consumers get the code and no type information, or types that only resolve under one configuration.

cards.q: How do you type an import of a non-JavaScript asset such as a CSS or SVG file?
cards.a: Declare the module pattern in a .d.ts included in the project — declare module '*.svg' { const src: string; export default src }.

cards.q: Your import works at runtime but the editor cannot find its types. Where do you look first?
cards.a: The package's exports map and types condition, then whether an @types package exists, then whether your moduleResolution matches the package's declared format.

cards.q: Why can an @types package be wrong?
cards.a: It is written by volunteers and versioned independently of the library, so it can describe an older or newer API than the one you installed.

cards.q: What are the three jobs tsconfig.json does?
cards.a: Says which files are in the project, what checking rules apply, and what output to produce.

cards.q: What determines which files are actually included?
cards.a: include, exclude and files — plus everything imported by an included file, whether or not you listed it.

cards.q: What does target control, and what does it not do?
cards.a: Which JavaScript version to emit, so newer syntax gets downlevelled. It does not add missing runtime APIs — no polyfills, ever.

cards.q: What is lib for?
cards.a: Which built-in API declarations to include, such as DOM for browser globals or ES2023 for newer standard library methods. It is why a method errors in one project and works in another.

cards.q: What is the cost of setting a low target?
cards.a: Bigger, slower, harder-to-debug output, because features like async/await get compiled into state machines instead of being emitted as written.

cards.q: What do paths and baseUrl do, and what is the trap?
cards.a: They teach the type-checker about import aliases such as @/lib/db. They do not affect runtime resolution, so a bundler or runtime resolver must be configured to match or the code type-checks and crashes on start.

cards.q: What does isolatedModules enforce and why?
cards.a: It forbids constructs that cannot be understood one file at a time, because esbuild, swc and similar tools compile each file in isolation and never see your types.

cards.q: What does skipLibCheck do and why is it almost always on?
cards.a: Skips type-checking declaration files in dependencies. Checking other people's declarations is slow and their errors are not yours to fix.

cards.q: What are project references and composite for?
cards.a: Splitting a repository into separately buildable units so a change in one package does not force rechecking everything, and so tsc --build can order the work.

cards.q: What does declarationMap add on top of declaration?
cards.a: Source maps for the declarations, so go-to-definition in a consuming project lands in your original TypeScript rather than in the generated .d.ts.

cards.q: What does extends in a tsconfig give you, and what is a good base?
cards.a: Shared configuration across several configs. The published @tsconfig/* bases are a reasonable starting point rather than copying settings you have not read.

cards.q: What is the single best mental model for tsconfig?
cards.a: It is not settings, it is the definition of the language dialect this repository speaks — which is why it is the first file to read in an unfamiliar codebase.

cards.q: Which flags are linting-adjacent rather than type-safety flags?
cards.a: noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters, noImplicitReturns and noFallthroughCasesInSwitch. They catch mistakes but are not about type soundness.

cards.q: What does incremental do and what does it write?
cards.a: Caches type information between runs in a .tsbuildinfo file so a second build only rechecks what changed.

cards.q: Your code type-checks but crashes with a module not found error at runtime. What is the likely cause?
cards.a: A paths alias known to the type-checker but not configured in the bundler or runtime resolver. The checker and the runtime resolve modules by separate mechanisms.

cards.q: A standard library method errors as not existing, though it works when you run it. What do you change?
cards.a: lib — the declarations for that version of the standard library are not included. Raising target usually raises the default lib as well.

cards.q: Why might the same file produce errors in CI and not locally?
cards.a: Different config resolution — a different tsconfig being picked up, a stale .tsbuildinfo, or different dependency versions supplying different declarations.

cards.q: What two jobs does tsc do, and why did the ecosystem split them?
cards.a: Type-checking and emitting. Checking is inherently slow because it builds a graph of every type; stripping types is nearly free. So fast tools transpile and tsc checks separately.

cards.q: Name the fast transpile-only tools and what they skip.
cards.a: esbuild (Go), swc (Rust), and wrappers such as tsx, Vite and Bun. They delete types and emit JavaScript in milliseconds and check nothing at all.

cards.q: What is the correct project setup for running and checking?
cards.a: A fast transpiler for running, tsc --noEmit in CI and as a pre-commit or pre-push check, and a real tsc build with declaration: true only if you publish a library.

cards.q: Why will your dev server happily run code with type errors?
cards.a: Because the transpiler never checks. The errors appear in your editor, not in the terminal, and if CI lacks a check step they reach main unnoticed.

cards.q: Why does isolatedModules matter specifically for transpilers?
cards.a: They see one file at a time, so re-exporting a type without export type is ambiguous to them even though tsc can resolve it from the whole program.

cards.q: What do you need for readable production stack traces?
cards.a: Source maps enabled at build time plus --enable-source-maps in Node or the source-map-support package. Without them every trace points at compiled line numbers.

cards.q: Why is a second tsc build much faster than the first?
cards.a: Watch mode and incremental reuse cached type information from .tsbuildinfo, so only changed files and their dependents are rechecked.

cards.q: Which build tool can generate .d.ts files?
cards.a: Only tsc (or tools that wrap it, such as some bundler plugins that shell out to it). This is the main reason a published package still needs a real TypeScript build.

cards.q: How would you set up CI so type errors cannot reach main?
cards.a: A required job running tsc --noEmit across the workspace, separate from the build and test steps so its failure is legible on its own.

cards.q: Your CI passes but the deployed app crashes on a type-level mistake. What was missing?
cards.a: A tsc --noEmit step. The build tool transpiled without checking, so nothing gated on type correctness.

cards.q: When is a real tsc build still required?
cards.a: When you publish a package and need .d.ts output, or when you rely on features a transpiler cannot implement in isolation.

cards.q: Why does a pre-push type check beat a pre-commit one in practice?
cards.a: Commits are frequent and often intermediate; pushes are the point where work becomes shared. Checking on push keeps the loop fast while still gating what others see.

cards.q: Why does const user: User = await res.json() compile despite validating nothing?
cards.a: res.json() returns Promise<any>, and any is assignable to User. The annotation is accepted as a claim and nothing is checked.

cards.q: State the rule about annotations on external data.
cards.a: A type annotation on external data is a lie until something validates it. Erasure means there is nothing at runtime to enforce the claim.

cards.q: What are the three honest ways to cross the runtime boundary?
cards.a: Hand-written type predicates, schema validation libraries such as Zod, and types generated from a source that describes itself such as OpenAPI or a database schema.

cards.q: Why do hand-written type predicates degrade over time?
cards.a: Nothing forces you to update the predicate when the type changes, so the check silently stops matching the type it claims to prove.

cards.q: What is the key inversion that makes Zod feel inevitable?
cards.a: The schema is a runtime value and the static type is derived from it with z.infer. One source of truth, validated at runtime and typed at compile time, and the two cannot drift.

cards.q: Why can't you just use an interface instead of a schema?
cards.a: An interface is erased, so it can describe the expected shape but can never check it. A schema exists at runtime and can.

cards.q: What is the trade-off with generated types?
cards.a: They give compile-time safety with no runtime cost, but only guarantee agreement at generation time — a stale generated file is its own failure mode.

cards.q: State the boundary rule for where to validate.
cards.a: Validate at the edges, trust in the interior. Parse everything entering the process, then work with typed values without defensive checks.

cards.q: Which specific boundaries should always be validated?
cards.a: HTTP handlers, queue consumers, process.env, file reads, third-party API responses, worker messages, and LLM tool-call arguments.

cards.q: How is process.env typed by default and why is that a problem?
cards.a: Record<string, string | undefined> — every variable is possibly undefined and always a string, so config errors surface at the moment a rare code path runs.

cards.q: What is the correct treatment of environment configuration?
cards.a: Parse the whole environment through a schema at startup so the process refuses to boot with a bad config, rather than failing later on one code path.

cards.q: Why is LLM output the purest example of untrusted data?
cards.a: It is produced by a probabilistic system that can return a plausible but wrong shape. It parses as JSON and satisfies no guarantee, so it must be validated before use like any external input.

cards.q: What does a repair loop look like for schema-validated LLM output?
cards.a: Parse with the schema; on failure, feed the validation error back to the model and retry a bounded number of times; on repeated failure, fall back to storing the raw input and flagging it.

cards.q: Why is validating everywhere as wrong as validating nowhere?
cards.a: Interior validation is noise that hides the real boundaries and slows everything, while adding no guarantee that the boundary check did not already provide.

cards.q: A file is named .pdf but its bytes are a JPEG. What is the general lesson?
cards.a: The declared type of external data is metadata written by someone else, exactly like a type annotation on a network response. The only truth is in the content, learned by inspection.

cards.q: Why is validating a worker message as important as validating an HTTP body?
cards.a: Messages are serialised and arrive as unknown, and the two sides can be built from different versions of the protocol. It is the same boundary in a different transport.

cards.q: What does z.infer actually give you?
cards.a: The static type that a schema's successful parse produces, computed from the schema at compile time so the runtime check and the static type cannot disagree.

cards.q: What is the difference between parse and safeParse in Zod, in type terms?
cards.a: parse throws and returns the typed value; safeParse returns a discriminated union of success and failure, which is the shape you want in a handler that must respond rather than crash.

cards.q: What is the goal of end-to-end type inference?
cards.a: One definition, with every other representation derived from it, so a change in one place produces compile errors everywhere that must change.

cards.q: How does Drizzle derive row types?
cards.a: Tables are defined as TypeScript values, so typeof users.$inferSelect is the row type and $inferInsert is the insert shape. The schema is the source and the types are computed.

cards.q: Why are $inferSelect and $inferInsert different?
cards.a: A row you read has generated columns such as id and timestamps; a row you write does not. The same entity has different shapes depending on the direction it crosses the boundary.

cards.q: How does Prisma differ from Drizzle in its typing approach?
cards.a: Prisma generates types from a separate schema file via a code-generation step; Drizzle infers them from TypeScript values directly. Both give one source of truth, but only one keeps it inside the type system.

cards.q: What does a Fastify type provider do?
cards.a: Connects a route's Zod or JSON schema to the types of request.body, params and reply, so declaring the schema types the handler and validates it from one declaration.

cards.q: Why do Express codebases often end up validated but untyped?
cards.a: Express types request bodies as any by default, so validation middleware can check the value at runtime without the handler's static type reflecting it.

cards.q: What is tRPC and what does it require?
cards.a: A way to share types across the client/server boundary by importing the server's router type into the client — no code generation, full autocomplete, at the cost of one TypeScript codebase on both sides.

cards.q: When is OpenAPI generation the right choice over type sharing?
cards.a: When the client is not yours or is not TypeScript, so a language-neutral contract with generated types is the only way both sides can agree.

cards.q: How does an LLM tool definition fit this pattern?
cards.a: The tool's JSON Schema and the type of the arguments you receive should both come from one Zod definition, and the returned arguments must still be validated because they are external data.

cards.q: State the general principle this node teaches.
cards.a: Pick one artifact as the source of truth and derive every other representation from it mechanically. Everything else in a large system's type story is an instance of that.

cards.q: What is the failure mode when this principle is not followed?
cards.a: The same entity is declared in the database, the API layer, the client and the tests, and the four copies drift silently until something breaks in production.

cards.q: Why does deriving types not eliminate the need for runtime validation?
cards.a: Derivation guarantees internal consistency, not that incoming data matches. The database and the client can agree perfectly while a third-party payload arrives in a different shape.

cards.q: You change a database column and want to know everything that breaks. What arrangement gives you that?
cards.a: Row types derived from the schema, API schemas derived from those, and client types derived from the API — then the compiler produces the list without you searching.

cards.q: Where do generated types fail you?
cards.a: When the generation step is stale or skipped in CI, the types describe a system that no longer exists and the compiler confidently confirms a false model.

cards.q: What is module augmentation and what makes it possible?
cards.a: Adding members to a type inside someone else's package, using declare module 'pkg'. It works because interfaces merge.

cards.q: Write the shape of a Fastify request augmentation.
cards.a: declare module 'fastify' { interface FastifyRequest { user?: AuthUser } } — after which every use site knows about the property.

cards.q: What does declare global do?
cards.a: Augments global types — extending Window, adding your variable names to ProcessEnv, or typing something injected by a script tag.

cards.q: What is the most common augmentation failure and why does it happen?
cards.a: Writing declare module in a file with no imports or exports, which declares a new ambient module instead of augmenting the existing one. The file must be a module.

cards.q: What is the second most common augmentation failure?
cards.a: The file is not included in the project, so nothing loads it. Augmentations placed in files nothing imports appear to do nothing at all.

cards.q: Why should an augmented property usually be optional?
cards.a: Because the augmentation is global and unconditional. Declaring user: AuthUser claims every request has one, including unauthenticated routes, which is exactly the false confidence you are trying to avoid.

cards.q: Which ecosystems depend on this mechanism?
cards.a: Fastify plugins and decorators, Express middleware via Express.Request, Next.js, Vitest matcher extensions — essentially every plugin system in the TypeScript world.

cards.q: Does declare global on ProcessEnv make your environment safe?
cards.a: No. It is a claim, not a check. Startup validation with a schema is what makes the claim true.

cards.q: Can type aliases be augmented the way interfaces are?
cards.a: No. Only interfaces (and namespaces) merge, which is the main practical reason libraries expose extension points as interfaces.

cards.q: What are the three dominant causes of slow type-checking?
cards.a: Large unions and their combinations, deep recursive conditional types, and inferred return types on exported functions that the checker must reconstruct at every use site.

cards.q: What does Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite usually mean?
cards.a: You have hit the recursion depth limit in a conditional or mapped type. It is usually a signal to simplify rather than to optimise.

cards.q: What is the single highest-leverage fix for compile speed in a library?
cards.a: Explicit return type annotations on exported functions, so the checker does not have to reconstruct a possibly enormous inferred type at every call site.

cards.q: Which tools tell you where compile time goes?
cards.a: tsc --diagnostics and --extendedDiagnostics for a summary, and --generateTrace for a profile you can open in a trace viewer.

cards.q: What structural options reduce repeat work?
cards.a: incremental with its .tsbuildinfo cache, and project references so unchanged packages are not rechecked.

cards.q: State the judgement rule this node exists to install.
cards.a: A type is only worth what it prevents. A clever type that catches a bug nobody would write, at the cost of a slow build and unreadable errors, is a net loss.

cards.q: What does senior-level TypeScript skill actually look like?
cards.a: Knowing which guarantees are worth their cost, keeping error messages legible, and being willing to use unknown plus a runtime check where the type-level version would be a monster.

cards.q: Why does an unreadable error message count as a real cost?
cards.a: Because the type exists to help a future developer, and a fifty-line error that nobody can parse consumes more time than the bug it prevented would have.

cards.q: Your editor becomes sluggish after adding a recursive type. What is the fastest diagnostic?
cards.a: Comment the type out and see whether responsiveness returns, then bound its depth or simplify. --generateTrace confirms it if you need evidence.

cards.q: When should you deliberately choose a runtime check over a type-level guarantee?
cards.a: When the type-level version is unreadable, slow, or produces errors no one can act on — the check still catches the bug and costs almost nothing to understand.

cards.q: What is native type stripping and where does it stand?
cards.a: Runtimes executing TypeScript by deleting the types. Node added --experimental-strip-types in Node 22 and made it on by default in Node 23; Deno and Bun run TypeScript directly.

cards.q: What does erasableSyntaxOnly do and why does it exist?
cards.a: Added in TypeScript 5.8, it errors on constructs that cannot simply be stripped — enums, parameter properties and namespaces — so your code stays compatible with type-stripping runtimes.

cards.q: What is the practical argument against enums now?
cards.a: It is no longer style. Enums emit runtime code, so they are incompatible with running TypeScript without a build step, which is where the ecosystem is heading.

cards.q: What is the Go port of the compiler?
cards.a: A rewrite of tsc in Go announced by Microsoft in 2025, targeting roughly ten-times-faster checking and better editor responsiveness, shipping as TypeScript 7 while the JavaScript compiler continues as 6.x.

cards.q: Name the notable recent additions to the language.
cards.a: satisfies (4.9), const type parameters and standard decorators (5.0), using and explicit resource management (5.2), NoInfer (5.4), and erasableSyntaxOnly (5.8).

cards.q: Why does upgrading TypeScript sometimes let you delete assertions?
cards.a: Narrowing and inference get smarter between versions, so code that genuinely needed an assertion two years ago may now be understood by the checker.

cards.q: Is TypeScript's type system sound?
cards.a: No, deliberately. Known holes include bivariant method parameters, type assertions, any, unchecked index access and mutable array covariance.

cards.q: What was TypeScript's actual design goal, given that unsoundness?
cards.a: Not to prove programs correct, but to catch the most bugs possible while staying usable on the JavaScript people actually write. Every hole is a conscious trade for that usability.

cards.q: Name three soundness holes and why each exists.
cards.a: Method bivariance, because array and DOM types depend on it; assertions, because sometimes you know more than the checker and migration requires an escape hatch; array covariance, because forbidding it breaks too much existing code.

cards.q: What has to be true of your code for it to run under Node type stripping?
cards.a: Only erasable syntax — no enums, no parameter properties, no namespaces — and imports that Node itself can resolve, since no bundler is involved.

cards.q: Does type stripping mean you no longer need tsc?
cards.a: No. Nothing is checked when types are stripped, so tsc --noEmit becomes more important, not less — it is the only thing standing between you and untyped JavaScript.
